--- title: "Regression diagnostics" author: "Dr. Yu Cheng Hsu" title-slide-attributes: data-background: /assets/images/lr/background-1.jpg data-background-size: 40% 100% data-background-position: right data-background-opacity: "0.8" format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../../../assets/css/general_style.css] slide-number: true smaller: true lightbox: true chalkboard: theme: whiteboard src: None lightbox: true bibliography: ref.bib engine: knitr --- ## Learning objectives - Demonstrate linear regression diagnostics - Judgement on the performance of linear regression Terms matching | Rachel's slide | Ray's slides | | ---- | --- | | $\text{SS}_\text{Total}$ | $\text{SST}$ | | $\text{SS}_\text{Regression}$ | $\text{SSR}$ | | $\text{SS}_\text{Residual}$ | $\text{SSE}$ | | $\text{MSS}_\text{Residual}$ | $\text{MSE}$ | :::{.aside} Background image: @bg1 ::: ## Overview of linear regression In linear regression, our fundamental objective is to explain the variability observed in the outcome variable ($Y$) using one or more explanatory variable ($X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k$). :::{.hide} $$ \hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_{1i} + b_2 X_{2i} + \dots + b_k X_{ki} $$ ::: It is crucial to know - Does $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k$ really make explaination to $Y$ - How good is the model performance? :::{.aside} (Note on terminology: In some literature, notably British and econometrics, SSR is termed "Explained Sum of Squares" (ESS) and SSE is termed "Residual Sum of Squares" (RSS). Always check definitions in your specific context). ::: ## Quick summary | Metric | Formula | Degrees of Freedom ($df$) | Conceptual Intuition | | :- | :-- | :-- | :------ | | **SST** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2$ | $n - 1$ | Total variation in the outcome $Y$ without using any predictors. | | **SSR** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2$ | $k$ | Variation accounted by the regression model. | | **SSE** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2$
$= \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$ | $n - k - 1$ | Unexplained variation; sum of squared discrepancies between observed points and regression surface. | :::{.aside} - $n$ represents the sample size - $k$ represents the number of predictors, excluding the intercept. ::: --- ## Goodness-of-Fit: $R^2$ $R^2$ (The coefficient of determination) quantifies the proportion of total variation in the response variable explained by the linear combination of predictors: :::{.hide} $$ R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}} $$ ::: **Interpretation Rules** - **Range:** In standard OLS with an intercept, $0 \le R^2 \le 1$ (or $0\%$ to $100\%$). - **Interpretation:** If $R^2 = 0.74$, exactly **74% of the variability in $Y$ is explained by the predictors** included in the model, while the remaining 26% is attributable to residual noise or omitted factors. - **Limitation:** $R^2$ is non-decreasing with respect to the addition of predictors. Adding completely unrelated random noise variables will force $\text{SSE}$ to stay equal or decrease, artificially inflating $R^2$. ## Adjusted $R^2$ ($R^2_{\text{adj}}$) The **Adjusted $R^2$** incorporates degrees of freedom to penalize excessive parameterization and prevent overfitting, : :::{.hide} $$ R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \left[ \frac{\text{SSE} / (n - k - 1)}{\text{SST} / (n - 1)} \right] = 1 - \left( \frac{\text{MSE}}{\text{MST}} \right) $$ ::: Alternatively expressed via $R^2$: $$ R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - k - 1} $$ **Key Properties** - Increases only if a newly added predictor reduces $\text{SSE}$ by a margin greater than what would be expected by pure chance. - Can occasionally yield a negative value when model fit is negligible; in such cases, it is effectively interpreted as zero. ## $F$-Test for Model Significance **$F$-Test** evaluates whether the collection of predictors collectively explains a statistically significant amount of variation. **Hypotheses** - **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** All slope coefficients are simultaneously zero. :::{.hide} $$ H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_k = 0 $$ ::: - **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$):** At least one slope coefficient is non-zero. :::{.hide} $$ H_1: \text{There is at least one} \beta_j \neq 0 $$ ::: **Difference on individual testing on $\beta_i$** - $\beta_i$ is a $t$-test - Repeated testing $\beta_i$ cause p-value inflation ## The Standard ANOVA Table for Regression Statistical software (e.g., R, Python `statsmodels`, Stata, SAS) formats these calculations into an ANOVA table: | Source of Variation | Sum of Squares ($SS$) | Degrees of Freedom ($df$) | Mean Square ($MS$) | $F$-Statistic | $p$-value | | :--- | :-- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Regression (Model)** | $\text{SSR}$ | $k$ | $\text{MSR} = \frac{\text{SSR}}{k}$ | $F = \frac{\text{MSR}}{\text{MSE}}$ | $P(F_{(k, n-k-1)} \ge F)$ | | **Residual (Error)** | $\text{SSE}$ | $n - k - 1$ | $\text{MSE} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n - k - 1}$ | — | — | | **Total** | $\text{SST}$ | $n - 1$ | $\text{MST} = \frac{\text{SST}}{n - 1}$ | — | — | --- ## Annotated Worked Example :::{.columns} :::{.column width=45%} Research purpose: Factors affecting infant birth weight ($n = 189$). - Outcome ($Y$): bwt (Infant birth weight in grams). ::: :::{.column width=52%} - Predictors ($X$): Maternal age (age), - maternal weight at last menstrual period (lwt), - smoking status during pregnancy (smoke), - history of hypertension (ht), - uterine irritability (ui) ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load MASS (pre-installed in R) library(MASS) data(birthwt) # Convert binary indicator variables into explicit factors birthwt$smoke <- factor(birthwt$smoke, labels = c("Non-Smoker", "Smoker")) birthwt$ht <- factor(birthwt$ht, labels = c("No", "Yes")) birthwt$ui <- factor(birthwt$ui, labels = c("No", "Yes")) ``` ::: ## Regression results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model <- lm(bwt ~ age + lwt + smoke + ht + ui, data = birthwt) summary(model) ``` ::: ```text Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1675.13 -464.38 -1.02 459.70 1779.69 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 2506.354 291.759 8.591 3.73e-15 *** age 3.648 9.432 0.387 0.69935 lwt 4.388 1.691 2.594 0.01024 * smokeSmoker -240.848 100.413 -2.399 0.01746 * htYes -643.958 207.232 -3.107 0.00219 ** uiYes -547.068 139.937 -3.909 0.00013 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 Residual standard error: 671.4 on 183 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1747, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1522 F-statistic: 7.75 on 5 and 183 DF, p-value: 1.234e-06 ``` ## ANOVA table ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(olsrr) olsaov<-ols_regress(model)$anova olsaov$anova ``` ::: ```text ANOVA ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Sum of Squares DF Mean Square F Sig. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Regression 17469477.719 5 3493895.544 7.75 0.0000 Residual 82500178.091 183 450820.645 Total 99969655.810 188 ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ``` ## Key Metrics Calculations 1. **$R^2$ Calculation:** $$ R^2 = \frac{17469477.719 }{ 99969655.810} = 17.4\% $$ *Interpretation:* 17.4% of the variance in biomarker reduction is explained by maternal weight at last menstrual period, baseline metabolic index, and age. 2. **Adjusted $R^2$ Calculation:** $$ R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \left( \frac{450820.645}{99969655.810/ 188} \right) = = 1 - 0.8478 = 15.2\% $$ *Interpretation:* After penalizing for adding three model parameters, the model accounts for approximately 70.2% of the variance. ## Common issues **Significant $F$-statistic, but no individual significant $t$-statistics** This classic paradox typically occurs due to **severe multicollinearity**. - The predictors are highly correlated with each other. - The overall $F$-test confirms that the set of predictors collectively accounts for substantial variation. **Low $R^2$ with a Statistically Significant $F$-test** - **Common in noisy biological or social science data** (e.g., $R^2 = 0.08$, $p < 0.001$ with $n = 5,000$). - This means the effect is genuine, real, and reproducible (not a sampling artifact), but individual-level variation remains high due to unmeasured factors. # L.I.N.E Assumptions ## Overview | Letter | Assumption | Primary Diagnostic Tool | |:------------------:|:----------------|:----------------|:----------------| | **L** | **Linearity** of the conditional expectation | $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid X] = 0$ | Residuals vs. Fitted Plot | | **I** | **Independence** of observational errors | $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0 \quad (\forall i \neq j)$ | Autocorrelation / Study Design Review | | **N** | **Normality** of error distribution | $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ | Normal Q-Q Plot | | **E** | **Equal Variance** (Homoscedasticity) | $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2$ (constant) | Scale-Location Plot | ## Pitfalls to Avoid 1. **Confusing $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ with Causality:** A high $R^2$ indicates strong linear correlation, not causal direction. 2. **Comparing $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ Across Different Transformations:** You cannot compare the $R^2$ of a model predicting $Y$ directly to a model predicting $\ln(Y)$, because $\text{SST}$ is measured on fundamentally different scales. 3. **Over-reliance on $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ Alone:** Always inspect residual diagnostics (residual vs. fitted plots, Q-Q plots) to ensure linearity, normality, and homoscedasticity assumptions hold. ## 4. In-Depth Diagnostics, Clinical Risks & Remedies ``` THE 4 BASE R DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS: plot(model) ┌───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐ │ 1. Residuals vs Fitted │ 2. Normal Q-Q Plot │ │ Checks: Linearity │ Checks: Normality │ │ Ideal: Flat red line at y = 0 │ Ideal: Points follow dashed 45°│ ├───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤ │ 3. Scale-Location │ 4. Residuals vs Leverage │ │ Checks: Equal Variance │ Checks: Influential Points │ │ Ideal: Flat horizontal line │ Ideal: Points inside Cook's d │ └───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ## L — Linearity - The relationship between $X$ and the outcome is an additive **linear** combination. **Example** - The relation between X and Y is a quadratic relation instead of a linear **Actions** - Add non-linear polynomial terms: e.g., $\text{Age}^2$. - Apply logarithmic or power transformations ## :::{.columns} **Tool:** **Residuals vs. Fitted Plot** :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(model, which = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} - **Healthy Pattern:** Residuals bounce randomly across a horizontal band centered at $y = 0$, with no distinct trend. The red smooth smoother curve is nearly flat along $y = 0$. - **Violation Warning:** Distinct parabolic "U-shape", inverted "U", or sinusoidal wave. ::: ::: ## I — Independence of Errors - Knowing that Patient A has an unexpectedly high outcome provides zero information about Patient B's outcome. - **Example** - Clustering: Patients recruited from the same hospital ward or family share correlated responses. - Autocorrelation: Longitudinal measurements taken repeatedly over time on the same subject. **Actions** - Revise study design - **Clustered data:** Linear Mixed-Effects Models (`lme4::lmer()`) incorporating random intercepts for clusters/centers. --- :::{.columns} - **Tool:** Evaluation of study design, Residuals vs. Time/Subject ID order, or **Durbin-Watson test** (`car::dwt(model)`). :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} car::dwt(model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lag Autocorrelation D-W Statistic p-value 1 0.7582327 0.4817912 0 Alternative hypothesis: rho != 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} **Consequence** - **Deceptive Precision:** The effective sample size is smaller than $n$. Linear regression underestimate standard errors ($SE(\hat{\beta})$), causing artificially narrow 95% CIs. ::: ::: ## N — Normality of Residuals - The error terms re normally distributed around the fitted line. **Crucial Clarification:** In regression, the raw variables $Y$ and $X$ **do not** need to be normally distributed; only the **residuals** ($\varepsilon_i$) must be normally distributed. - **Tool:** **Normal Q-Q Plot** (Base R Plot 2: `plot(model, which = 2)`). - **Healthy Pattern:** Residual quantiles fall tightly along the theoretical 45-degree dashed line. **Actions** - Transform the outcome variable: logarithmic transformation: $$\log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i$$ ## :::{.columns} :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(model, which = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} - **Violation Warning:** - **Heavy tails (S-shape):** Data has far more extreme clinical outliers than predicted by a normal curve. - **Curvature at ends:** Skewed distributions (frequently seen with right-skewed lab markers such as serum creatinine, viral loads, or cytokine concentrations). ::: ::: ## E — Equal Variance - The variance of the residuals $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2$ is constant across all predicted values $\hat{Y}$. (Homoscedasticity) **Consequence** - Conventional $SE(\hat{\beta})$ calculations are invalid. If variance expands at higher values, standard errors are underestimated for higher exposures, leading to false claims of significance. **Actions** 1. **Variance-stabilizing transformations:** $\log(Y)$ or $\sqrt{Y}$. 2. **Heteroscedasticity-Consistent (HC) Robust Standard Errors:** Using `sandwich::vcovHC(model, type = "HC3")` paired with `lmtest::coeftest()`. 3. **Weighted Least Squares (WLS):** Weights inversely proportional to variance: $w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2$. ## :::{.columns} :::{.column} - **Tool:** **Scale-Location Plot** (Base R Plot 3: `plot(model, which = 3)`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(model, which = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Linear-regression_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} - **Healthy Pattern:** A horizontal smooth red line with an even, constant vertical scatter of points across all fitted values. - **Violation Warning:** A **megaphone / funnel shape** where residual spread widens drastically as $\hat{Y}$ increases (common in biomedical dosing and growth studies). ::: ::: ## Summary Diagnostic Flowchart ```text [Fit Linear Model: lm(Y ~ X1 + X2)] │ ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ [Evaluate Goodness-of-Fit] [Validate L.I.N.E.] • R² & Adjusted R² • Residuals vs Fitted (Linearity) • Residual Std Error (RSE) • Study structure (Independence) • Global ANOVA F-Test • Normal Q-Q (Normality) │ • Scale-Location (Equal Variance) │ │ └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘ │ All L.I.N.E. Assumptions Hold? │ ├─── YES ──► Report slopes, 95% CIs & p-values │ └─── NO ──► Apply Diagnostic Remedy: • Non-linear? ──► Log(X), Polynomials • Heteroscedastic? ──► Log(Y), HC3 Robust SE • Non-normal? ──► Transform Y, Bootstrap • Clustered? ──► Mixed-Effects Model (lmer) ```

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
